title: Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training (GPT-1)
authors: Alec Radford, Karthik Narasimhan, Tim Salimans, Ilya Sutskever

pages.title: Pre-train a Transformer LM, fine-tune on downstream tasks

blocks.html: The problem. Labeled data in NLP is scarce and expensive: someone has to hand-annotate sentiment, entailment, or answers. Meanwhile, raw unlabeled text — books, web pages — is effectively unlimited and free. Before this paper, models were typically trained task-by-task from scratch, sometimes warm-started with word embeddings (word2vec, GloVe) that capture single-word meaning but nothing about how words combine in context. The motivating question: can we do most of the learning on cheap unlabeled text, then adapt cheaply to each labeled task?
The two-stage recipe. GPT-1's answer — now the template for the entire field — has two stages:

items: Stage 1, generative pre-training: train a Transformer decoder on a large unlabeled corpus (BooksCorpus — ~7,000 unpublished books, ~800M words) with a plain next-word language-modeling objective.
Stage 2, discriminative fine-tuning: take that pre-trained model, add a small task-specific input transformation and one extra linear layer, and fine-tune the whole model on each labeled task.

blocks.html: Why books, not random web text? The authors specifically chose BooksCorpus because books contain long stretches of contiguous text, which lets the model learn to condition on long-range dependencies — something you can't learn from shuffled, sentence-level corpora.

The result. One pre-trained model, fine-tuned per task, improved the state of the art on 9 of 12 NLP datasets at release — beating architectures hand-designed for each individual task. This was the first demonstration that a single, task-agnostic, generatively pre-trained Transformer could be a strong starting point across the board.

Historical note. GPT-1 is the seed of the entire GPT line. The decoder-only autoregressive Transformer and the pre-train-then-adapt methodology introduced here, scaled up, became GPT-2, GPT-3, GPT-4, and the modern chat-model industry. BERT (months later) took the same pre-training idea in the bidirectional direction.

The idea. Teach the model to predict the next word, over and over, across a huge corpus. To do that well, a model must implicitly learn grammar, facts, coreference, and a great deal of world knowledge — all of which become useful for downstream tasks. This is left-to-right (autoregressive) language modeling: at each position you may only look at the words that came before.

A concrete example. Given the context “The cat sat on the”, the model outputs a probability distribution over the whole vocabulary, ideally with high mass on mat, floor, chair. The training signal is simply: maximize the probability assigned to the word that actually came next in the book.

Reading it term by term: $\mathcal{U} = \{u_1, \ldots, u_n\}$ is the corpus of tokens; for each position $i$ the model predicts $u_i$ from the $k$ preceding tokens $u_{i-k}, \ldots, u_{i-1}$ (here $k$ is the context window size); $\Theta$ are the network's parameters; $P$ is the model's predicted probability. We sum $\log P$ over all positions and maximize it — equivalently, minimize the cross-entropy of predicting each next token. No labels are needed; the corpus supervises itself.

The architecture. GPT-1 is a 12-layer Transformer decoder — the masked-self-attention variant, where each token can only attend to earlier positions (this masking is what enforces left-to-right). 12 attention heads, hidden size $H = 768$, feed-forward inner dimension 3072, about 117M parameters. Tokenization is byte-pair encoding (BPE) with 40,000 merges, and the position embeddings are learned (not the original Transformer's fixed sinusoids). It was trained for 100 epochs on BooksCorpus.

From predicting words to predicting labels. Once pre-training has produced a model full of linguistic knowledge, fine-tuning re-purposes it for a supervised task. Feed the task input through the pre-trained Transformer, grab the final hidden state of the last token, and run it through one new linear layer to predict the label.

$x^1, \ldots, x^m$ are the input tokens; $h_l^m$ is the final-layer ($l$) hidden vector at the last token position ($m$); $W_y$ is the only new parameter matrix, projecting that vector onto the label set; softmax turns it into a class distribution. The supervised objective is to maximize the log-probability of the correct label over the labeled dataset $\mathcal{C}$:

A clever stabilizer. The authors found that also keeping the language-modeling objective active during fine-tuning helps. The combined objective is $L_3(\mathcal{C}) = L_2(\mathcal{C}) + \lambda \, L_1(\mathcal{C})$, where $\lambda$ is a small weight on the auxiliary LM term. Continuing to predict next-words while learning the task (a) acts as a regularizer that improves generalization, and (b) prevents the model from catastrophically forgetting the broad knowledge it gained in pre-training as it specializes. Fine-tuning is fast — typically just 3 epochs were enough for most tasks.

pages.title: Turning every task into a single sequence

blocks.html: The problem. Tasks have different shapes. Sentiment classification takes one sentence; entailment takes a (premise, hypothesis) pair; multiple-choice QA takes a context plus several candidate answers. The old approach was to design a custom architecture for each shape. GPT-1's pre-trained model, though, only knows how to process one contiguous sequence of tokens. How do you feed it a pair, or a set of choices?

The traversal-style trick. Convert every structured input into a single ordered sequence using special delimiter tokens — a [start] token, a [delim] separator, and an [extract] end token whose final hidden state feeds the classifier. The pre-trained model is left structurally untouched; only the input formatting changes.

items: Similarity: order matters to a left-to-right model, so feed both orderings — [start] A [delim] B [extract] and [start] B [delim] A [extract] — and add (element-wise sum) the two final representations before classifying.
Multiple choice / QA: for each candidate, feed [start] context [delim] choice_i [extract]; produce a scalar per choice; softmax over the choices to pick one.

blocks.html: Why it matters. This “turn everything into a sequence of text and let the same model read it” framing is profound. It is the direct ancestor of the way GPT-2, GPT-3, and modern chat models work — where the task itself is described in the text rather than baked into a separate architecture. GPT-1 still needed a tiny per-task linear head; GPT-3 would later drop even that.
GPT-1 improved the state of the art on 9 of 12 evaluated datasets, spanning four task families — all from a single pre-trained model with a swapped last layer.

items: Natural language inference (does A entail B?): big gains on MNLI, SNLI, SciTail, QNLI, and RTE — e.g. +1.5% on MNLI, +5% on SciTail, +5.8% on QNLI over prior SOTA.

Question answering & commonsense: +8.9% on Story Cloze and +5.7% on the RACE reading-comprehension benchmark — the largest jumps, which the authors attribute to BooksCorpus teaching long-range reasoning.
Semantic similarity / paraphrase: new SOTA on QQP (+4.2%) and STS-B; competitive on MRPC.
Classification: a striking result on CoLA (linguistic acceptability), 45.4 vs. the previous 35.0 — a sign the model had absorbed real grammatical structure — and strong SST-2 sentiment.

blocks.html: The headline. Earlier systems needed bespoke architectures and ad-hoc embeddings per task. GPT-1 needed one model and a different last layer — a dramatic simplification, and one of the first clear signs that general pre-training could outperform task-specific engineering.

pages.title: Ablations: what actually drove the gains

blocks.html: The authors ran careful ablations (removing one component to measure its contribution) to attribute the success. Three findings stand out.

items: Pre-training is essential. The same Transformer trained from scratch on each task — no pre-training — drops the average score across tasks from ~74.7 to ~59.9, a ~15-point collapse. Pre-training does the heavy lifting.

More transferred layers help. Transferring more of the pre-trained layers (rather than just the embeddings) raises downstream performance nearly monotonically — up to ~9% on MultiNLI — because each layer carries reusable functionality.

The Transformer beats an LSTM. Swapping the Transformer for a comparable single-layer LSTM drops the average by ~5.6 points, and the LSTM only wins on one tiny dataset (MRPC). The bidirectional-context-free architecture genuinely matters, not just the pre-training.

blocks.html: The auxiliary LM loss has a size-dependent effect: it helps on larger datasets (like MNLI and QQP) but mildly hurts on smaller ones — consistent with it acting as a regularizer that big-data tasks can afford and small-data tasks find too constraining.

Zero-shot behaviors. In an early hint of what GPT-3 would later make central, the authors probed the pre-trained-only model (no fine-tuning) using heuristic prompts and watched its zero-shot task performance climb steadily over the course of pre-training. The interpretation: generative pre-training teaches a wide range of task-relevant abilities as a side effect, and the Transformer surfaces them far better than an LSTM does. Few-shot/zero-shot prompting would become the whole story two model generations later.

The lineage. GPT-1 introduced the recipe — decoder-only autoregressive Transformer, generatively pre-trained on a huge unlabeled corpus, then adapted to downstream tasks — that, scaled up, became GPT-2 (1.5B params, 2019), GPT-3 (175B, 2020), GPT-4 (2023), and the entire modern LLM industry. Two specific choices made here flow straight through: the architecture (decoder-only, autoregressive) and the methodology (pre-train at scale, adapt cheaply).

The fork in the road. BERT, released months later, took the same pre-training insight in the opposite direction — bidirectional masked language modeling on a Transformer encoder — and won the understanding-task leaderboards GPT-1 had topped. For a few years the field split into the encoder-only (BERT) camp for understanding and the decoder-only (GPT) camp for generation. The decoder-only line ultimately won the broader argument, because once models were large enough, generation-style models could also do understanding tasks via prompting — the seed of which is already visible in GPT-1's zero-shot experiments.

Connection to this collection. Read GPT-1 as the origin point and BERT as its bidirectional sibling; GPT-3 (also here) is GPT-1 scaled ~1500x with the fine-tuning step removed; DistilBERT shows the compression side of the same deployment problem.
